text: The fight this film cares about takes place at a table, over paperwork, rather than under lights in a ring. Rubin Carter was a boxer, and the nickname stayed with him into a murder conviction he spent years contesting; Norman Jewison gives most of 146 minutes to what that contesting actually consists of — letters, visits, a case file read by people under no obligation to open it. It is mainstream American filmmaking and makes no secret of wanting a large audience, which shapes the telling: clear antagonists, a clear moral line, momentum where a legal process would supply delay. The performance at the centre has to carry the years a courtroom scene cannot show, and the film is built to give it room. What it asks in return is patience with a story whose decisive events are documents.

Chuck Barris produced game shows, and said that between tapings he worked as an assassin for the CIA. The film takes him at his word and simultaneously refuses to, which may be the only honest way to shoot a memoir that ends in a shrug: the studio floor lit like a studio floor, the killings arriving with the timing of a punchline, neither register conceding to the other. George Clooney directs, and the tonal instability is the design rather than a flaw in it — comedy, crime and a love story compressed into 113 minutes with none of them willing to serve as the frame. Whether Barris was lying interests the picture less than what sort of man requires that particular lie, and it keeps circling back to that in the middle of the jokes.

A court physician is paid to stand nearer the body of power than anyone else in the building. En kongelig affære turns that access into a political crisis: a young queen, foreign to the court and bored in the particular way a life of ceremony produces, and a doctor with theories about how a kingdom ought to be governed. Romance arrives here as a political act before it is a private one, which is why Nikolaj Arcel spends his 137 minutes on how a decree gets drafted and who is standing nearby when it does, rather than on spectacle. The Danish dialogue is unhurried and the palace stays cold; the production design took a European Film Award and earns it in candlelight, corridors, and the number of people within earshot of any given sentence.

Most of the film is a man walking out into the fields around Arles and looking at them for longer than is comfortable. At Eternity's Gate treats Vincent van Gogh's last years as a matter of eyesight and weather rather than biography: the camera goes handheld and low, light smears, the bottom of the frame blurs, and the effect stops being a technique and starts being a report on how the world arrives for one particular pair of eyes. Julian Schnabel keeps it to 111 minutes and declines most of the scenes a life story is expected to supply. What remains is labour — canvas carried across open ground, boots, the physical nuisance of painting outdoors in wind — and the difficulty of explaining a way of seeing to people who do not share it.

The hitman thriller runs on competence: the man knows the building, the exits, and what he did last night. Memory removes the last item. Alex turns down a contract, becomes a target of the organisation that hired him and of the FBI at once, and has to work the problem while his recall comes apart — he cannot verify his own account of yesterday, let alone anyone else's, so every person on screen stays unconfirmed. Martin Campbell directs it as a chase with a leak in it, 114 minutes, the set pieces arranged so that a man who forgets is still quick enough to survive the next five minutes. The pleasure is structural rather than psychological: a genre built on trusting the protagonist's judgement, deliberately withdrawing the grounds for that trust.

Poppy is delighted by almost everything, and the people around her have trouble forgiving it. She teaches primary school in North London, and her cheer is not a mask waiting to slip, which is the real provocation, since the form usually treats good humour as either ignorance or a symptom. Mike Leigh gives 118 minutes to a few months of an ordinary life and refuses to organise them into a lesson — episodes, conversations, a job, rooms, people talking past one another at length. The comedy comes from watching a temperament meet resistance. The drama comes from noticing that her optimism is a practice, kept up at some cost, rather than a failure to understand what the world is like. It is a heavily written film working hard to seem unwritten.

The case is closed almost as soon as it opens, which is what makes a private detective useful to whoever wants it reopened. George Reeves dies at home; Louis Simo takes the job of asking why, and the asking carries him into a studio executive's marriage, where the answers belong to people wealthy enough to keep them. Allen Coulter is less interested in producing a solution than in what an industry does with a death — who makes the telephone call, who gets protected, what a career looks like from outside once it has stopped moving. It is based on a true story, and the film treats that phrase as a constraint to work inside rather than a licence. 126 minutes of a hired man entering rooms where everyone present has already agreed what happened.

Bolivia, seven years after Cuba, and almost nothing carries over. Che: Part Two is the half of Steven Soderbergh's project in which a method that worked once is tried in a country where the response is the entire question — the same discipline, the same columns moving through the same kind of undergrowth, none of the conditions that held the first time. Soderbergh shoots it as logistics: radios, boots, supply, the daily arithmetic of a column operating in country that is not its own. Where a life like this usually attracts speeches, this one keeps to procedure, and 135 minutes accumulate into something closer to a report filed from inside a plan under strain. What the film knows, it knows through terrain and equipment.

The household is a biker club, and the teenager at its centre does his homework. He is bright, funny and severely disfigured, and the film's working assumption is that the third fact is the least interesting of the three — an assumption it has to keep proving, since everyone he meets outside the house arrives at them in the opposite order. Peter Bogdanovich puts the weight on his mother, a woman with her own appetites and her own unreliability, who fights on his behalf against institutions rather than villains. The makeup took an Academy Award, an odd honour for work designed to stop being the subject after twenty minutes. Two hours in an American town, largely domestic, more concerned with what an ordinary week costs this family than with arranging a crisis.

Everything is fastened: collars, doors, and the sentences people use when they are saying something they cannot say. Maurice runs 140 minutes inside Edwardian manners, and the manners are the mechanism rather than the decoration — a young man works out what he wants in a society that has arranged its rooms, its friendships and its vocabulary so that the working-out has nowhere to occur. James Ivory takes the long form seriously; the pace allows for the gap between what a conversation is and what it is about, which is where most of the film lives. The costume design won an Academy Award and does genuine work, since class and permission are legible in cloth here before anyone speaks. A rejection starts it. What follows is the slower question of how to live.

A teenager still sucks his thumb, and the adults around him treat it as a problem awaiting the correct intervention. Thumbsucker moves Justin Cobb through suburban Oregon, a diagnosis and a prescription, and its subject is less the habit than the apparatus that assembles around it: a name for the trouble, a drug for the name, a household rearranged to accommodate both. Mike Mills keeps to 96 minutes and stays close to the comedy of parents who are themselves unfinished and of helpers arriving with theories of their own. A Sundance jury prize went to the acting, which suits a picture built on close attention to one face while other people adjust its chemistry. The sympathy is spread evenly, including toward the adults getting it wrong.

Needle Park is a patch of Manhattan with benches, and the film treats it as a place of business: waiting, scoring, the hours that go into keeping a habit supplied. Bobby hustles small. Helen has nowhere else to be, and what she finds in him is a routine to attach herself to, which the film is honest enough to call love without upgrading it into anything else. 1971, 110 minutes, and the New York around them is documentary-plain — streets used as streets, no arc that turns addiction into a lesson. The attention goes to economics and time: what a day costs, who owes whom, how long it takes to cross a city with money that has to last. The romance is conducted in those intervals, between errands, and it is the warmest thing in the frame.

In 1943, one hundred and thirty thousand men from France's colonies put on French uniforms to liberate a country none of them had set foot in. Indigènes follows four of them — Said, Abdelkader, Messaoud and Yassir — and its subject is the distance between the uniform and the standing that comes with it. Rachid Bouchareb films the fighting plainly and saves the pressure for everything around it: the units, the orders, the quiet business of who counts. At 128 minutes this is a war picture organised around accounting rather than courage, and the men in it have volunteered for a fatherland that files them under another word. The title stays in French, which is the charge: it is made in the language of the army that did the classifying.

A ski accident puts Tony in a rehabilitation centre, dependent on the staff and on painkillers, and the schedule there is what finally gives her time to go back over Georgio. Maïwenn builds the film on that rhyme and declines to press it: a body slowly rebuilt, a relationship slowly reopened, both processes carried out in rooms with other people in them. The account is partial by design, since it comes from someone with reasons to tell it a particular way, and the film lets the man's charm survive alongside the damage instead of settling the case. 125 minutes, largely two faces. The Cannes prize for the lead performance is the one worth naming, because what the story withholds is carried in a face at work on a knee.
